text: 1 Introduction

We study the problem of sampling from a centered Gaussian distribution given query access to its unnormalized density. Gaussian sampling is a fundamental algorithmic task with applications in Bayesian inference [ 7 ] , numerical simulation [ 11 ] , and randomized approximation algorithms [ 16 ] .

The target is $\pi_{A}=N(0,A^{-1})$ , where the unknown precision matrix $A$ satisfies $I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}$ . An algorithm accesses $A$ through matrix–vector product queries. At each step, it chooses a vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and observes $Ax$ . The goal of the algorithm is to output a random vector whose distribution is within $\varepsilon$ of $\pi_{A}$ in total variation (TV) distance. We ask how many queries required for sampling from $d$ -dimensional Gaussian distribution to accuracy $\varepsilon$ with the condition number $\kappa$ .

Gaussian sampling has a long history, with methods based on polynomial approximations to matrix square roots and inverse square roots [ 13 , 12 ] , Krylov subspaces and conjugate gradients [ 23 , 4 , 11 ] , and Markov chain Monte Carlo, including Gibbs sampling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [ 25 , 14 , 2 ] . In the first-order oracle model considered here, [ 17 ] obtained a query bound of $O(\kappa d\log^{3}(\tfrac{\kappa d}{\varepsilon}))$ for Metropolized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. For Gaussian targets, [ 2 ] improved this to $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\,d^{1/4}\log(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}))$ using long, randomized integration times, with initialization included in the query count. Analyses of Hit-and-Run also yield an $O(\kappa d\log(\tfrac{\kappa d}{\varepsilon}))$ query bound, since each exact Gaussian line update requires only one matrix-vector query [ 3 , 8 ] . A sharper worst-case upper bound is provided by the polynomial sampler of [ 10 ] , which requires $O(\min\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\tfrac{d}{\varepsilon})\})$ queries for total variation error $\varepsilon$ . At a sufficiently small constant total variation error, they proved a lower bound of $\Omega(\min\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\})$ against arbitrary randomized adaptive algorithms. They further obtained $\Omega_{\delta}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ when $\kappa\leq d^{1/5-\delta}$ , for any fixed $\delta\in(0,1/5)$ , matching their upper bound at constant accuracy in this regime. They conjectured that $\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ queries are necessary whenever $\sqrt{\kappa}\log d\leq d$ . A recent preprint [ 22 ] gives an $\Omega(\log d)$ lower bound for $\kappa=2$ and $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{10}$ , using instances with a fixed spectrum and a random eigenbasis. None of these lower bounds grows as $\varepsilon\to 0$ , and for $\kappa\geq d^{1/5}$ they are below the upper bound by a factor of order $\log(d/\varepsilon)$ .

However, both regimes arise in applications. Large condition numbers arise naturally in spatial statistics and Gaussian process regression [ 1 , 6 , 18 ] . On a bounded domain, the covariance matrices of a fixed Matérn model satisfy $\kappa=\Omega(d)$ as the number $d$ of sampling locations increases [ 26 ] . Sparse precision matrices arising from SPDE-based Gaussian Markov random field approximations of Mat’ern fields can likewise become ill-conditioned under mesh refinement [ 19 , 24 ] . For example, a regular-grid discretization of the Matérn SPDE with $\nu=1$ on a fixed two-dimensional periodic domain satisfies $\kappa=\Theta(d^{2})$ under uniform refinement.

High sampling accuracy matters for estimating a rare failure probability $p$ [ 20 ] , since TV error $\varepsilon$ allows relative bias up to $\varepsilon/p$ . High accuracy matters in Gibbs samplers with Gaussian conditionals [ 7 , 21 ] , where uncorrected sampling errors can bias the chain [ 15 ] . From a common initial law, a uniform per-update TV error of $\varepsilon$ accumulates to at most $N\varepsilon$ over $N$ updates. In neither regime do the known bounds determine the query complexity. This leads to the following question.
Can we establish sharp lower bounds for high-accuracy sampling from ill-conditioned Gaussians, uniformly over all dimensions ?
1.1 Our results
Our first result is the following lower bound, which holds for every $\kappa\geq 4$ and increases as $\varepsilon$ decreases to zero.

Theorem 1.1 (Informal; see Theorem 3.1 ) .

For every integer $d\geq 1$ , $\kappa\geq 4$ , and $0<\varepsilon\leq 1/16$ , any Gaussian sampler requires $\Omega\big(\min\big\{d,\,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\big(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\big)\big\}\big)$ queries.

Our lower bound matches the known upper bound of $O\!\big(\min\big\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\tfrac{d}{\varepsilon})\big\}\big)$ up to constant factors whenever $\kappa\leq d^{2-\delta}$ for any fixed $\delta\in(0,2)$ . At constant accuracy, the two bounds were previously known to match only for $\kappa\leq d^{1/5-\delta}$ . This confirms the conjecture of [ 10 ] that $\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ queries are necessary at constant accuracy whenever $\sqrt{\kappa}\log d\leq d$ . It also matches the upper bound for every $\kappa\geq 4$ whenever $\varepsilon\leq d^{-c}$ for any fixed $c>0$ . For $\kappa\geq d^{2}$ , it yields the optimal $\Theta(d)$ query complexity.

We also extend the hidden-eigenbasis construction of [ 22 ] to obtain an $\Omega_{\delta}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ lower bound for $2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ . We summarize the comparisons in Table 1 .
Theorem 1.2 (Informal; see Theorem 4.1 ) .

For every fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$ , sufficiently large $d$ , $2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}$ , and $0<\varepsilon\leq 1/10$ , any Gaussian sampler requires $\Omega_{\delta}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ queries.

This bound is tight at constant accuracy and, more generally, whenever $d^{-C}\leq\varepsilon\leq 1/10$ for a fixed $C>0$ , with matching constants depending on $\delta$ and $C$ . For $\kappa\geq 4$ and $\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{16}$ it is implied by Theorem 3.1 while the new cases are $2\leq\kappa<4$ and $\frac{1}{16}<\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{10}$ . We include it because its hard instances have a fixed spectrum, so the bound holds even for algorithms that know the spectrum of the precision matrix. Section 4.4 explains why the analysis of these instances gives no dependence on $\varepsilon$ and does not extend beyond $\kappa=d^{1-\delta}$ .
Remark 1.3 ( Connection to strongly log-concave sampling).

Our lower bounds also apply to sampling from $\pi\propto e^{-V}$ with $I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq\kappa I_{d}$ using exact value-and-gradient queries, even when the minimizer is known. For $\kappa=2$ and TV accuracy $1/10$ , [ 22 ] establishes an $O_{\eta}(d^{\eta})$ upper bound for every fixed $\eta>0$ , leaving a gap from the $\Omega(\log d)$ lower bound, whereas Gaussian sampling has complexity $\Theta(\log d)$ in this regime. For general condition numbers and high accuracy, [ 9 ] obtain TV error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\,d^{1/4}\operatorname{polylog}(1/\varepsilon))$ expected gradient queries with a warm start. Thus, our results provide an improved lower bounds for general strongly log-concave sampling with almost tight lower bounds for Gaussian subclass.
